chapter_theme: Civakan crosses from the marutam country through the hills and pastures to the grove of Vanagiri, where a woman like a celestial tries her charms on him; reading her intent, he meditates to his heart on the death that ends a lover's pleasures and on the body as a hut of flesh built by the deed, and she, to move him, tells that a Vidyadhara carried her off and his wife cast her into the forest, giving her name as Anangamaa Veenai.

cast.role: the hero, travelling alone after leaving Kemasari
Civakan's own heart, which he addresses as he reflects
the woman who appears to Civakan in the Vanagiri grove and says a Vidyadhara carried her off
the Vidyadhara who, by her account, abducted Anangamaa Veenai
the Vidyadhara's wife, who by her account had her thrown into the forest
the hill women who give food to travellers

1557.reading: Like men who leave behind the stage dancers with their girdles and red lips and the loving wife of the house, Civakan gives up the marutam land of sweet waters, where peacock flocks call, and sets out for the hard wasteland that smells of the musth of tree-felling elephants.
1557.nuance: The simile for his leaving is the man who renounces both courtesan and wife (அன்பின் மனையவள் துறந்து செல்பவர்), set just after he has left Kemasari in the night; the word துறந்து looks ahead to the renunciation the patikam promises.
1557.event: Civakan sets out from the marutam country into the wasteland.

1558.reading: The kaya blossoms on the peacock's neck-like slopes, the kongu trees flower like men wearing bright crowns on the king's festival day, and the maravam trees flower together like the chamberlains in cloth turbans who walk behind them.
1558.nuance: The forest is described in the terms of a royal procession, so the landscape the hero walks through is dressed as the court he will later rule.

1559.reading: Great honeycombs broken by mountain goats on the high hills spill and run down the sandalwood trunks, like the red-gold chain that plays on the chest of Vishnu who holds the discus and conch.

1560.reading: Waterfalls on the cloud-crossed peaks look like great snakes shedding their skins, beat like drums as they fall, and to the bees' song the peacocks gather and dance a drama.

1561.reading: Millet with heads hanging like honeycombs, avarai pods in clusters like an elephant's ripe fruit, hill rice, sugarcane, varagu, white gram, black gram and other crops grow there without limit.

1562.reading: Along every stretch of the road, doe-eyed women give travellers hill rice pounded with an ivory pestle in a rock mortar, honey, sweet plantains and fresh millet cakes that melt those who eat them.
1562.nuance: The giving is the hill people's, not the hero's: the road itself is a place of hospitality.
1562.event: The hill women give food to those who pass along the road.

1563.reading: Leaving the bounds of the kurinji, the mullai land appears: the jasmine creeper dances as if speaking, the kuravam offers its flower-dolls to the golden konrai, the tonri holds up its lamp, and bees hum as the full kurundham drips honey.
1563.event: Civakan passes from the hill country into the forest-pasture land.

1564.reading: With cochineal insects spread over the crops like lac-dyed cotton on an emerald board, herdsmen with curd-smeared hair playing sweet flutes and the cattle bells ringing, the tall one crosses the long land.

1565.reading: There appears the mountain Vanagiri, where gold and diamonds glitter in the pits dug for valli roots, and whose leaping waterfalls look like strands of white silver fastened from sky to ground.
1565.nuance: The waterfalls seem to set out to enter heaven (துறக்கம் புக்கிடும் என); the name of the mountain is given here, ahead of the grove in which the meeting takes place.

1566.reading: Ahead of where he goes lies a flowering grove with a pool as clear as washed gems, crowded with lotus, red lily, blue lily and white water lily, with bees humming like bards.

1567.reading: Going through the forest, he sees the beauty of the fragrant grove and sits down there, and at once a young woman like a daughter of the gods come down from the sky stands near him, breathing scent of musk, flowers and sandal.
1567.event: Civakan sits in the grove and a woman like a celestial appears and stands near him.

1568.reading: Her breasts dressed in saffron and her garland like kurinji flowers, she shows her golden girdle, lifts one edge of her long cloth, pinches a flower without flicking it, sends her glance as a messenger like fragrant smoke and stands with her smiling face turned aside.
1568.event: The woman shows herself to him with signs of invitation.

1569.reading: Drawn by the sound of her ornaments and her nectar-like scent, he turns his broad neck with a lion's look and sees with his eyes the one of matchless grace standing in the shade of the naga, vazhai and maravam trees.
1569.event: Civakan turns and sees the woman.

1570.reading: When his eyes meet hers she trembles, her earrings flash as she sways like a shaken creeper and her fine cloth slips, and he, looking all around, asks whether she is a yakshi.
1570.nuance: இயக்கி (a yakshi) is his first guess at what the forest beauty is; the epic leaves it as his guess, and in 1580 she gives another account of herself.
1570.event: Civakan, seeing her tremble, wonders aloud whether she is a yakshi.

1571.reading: While he sits holding the thought that she is a yakshi, she stands with her flower-eyes as arrows and her brow as a bow, as if to shoot at the man of inner restraint, ripe with a woman's beauty.
1571.nuance: உண்ணிறை உடைய, 'having inner restraint', is said of the target: the hero's nirai is what she aims at.

1572.reading: Without letting her smile show first, with eyes like a bud split open, hair in short curls and her small brow raised as her cloth slips, she lets fly even Ananga's five arrows that pierce the lives of the knowing.
1572.event: The woman tries her charms on Civakan.

1573.reading: As the woman with eyes like split mango stands looking like a doll in a picture drawn by a master, the hero with the ringing golden anklet sees her innocent intent and thinks this in his mind.
1573.event: Civakan reads her intent and begins to reflect.

1574.reading: He asks his heart whether this world is good, where men who wore garlands, dabbed camphor and lay on the shoulders of soft-breasted women at their last evening have their eyes closed by those same women and go.
1574.nuance: The metre changes to a venba-like quatrain, and the refrain நெஞ்சே, kept through 1576, turns the hero's reply to temptation into a meditation addressed to himself; the women's hands that caressed are the hands that close the dead man's eyes.

claims.claim: the pleasures of women in this world end at death, when the beloved herself closes the lover's eyes, so the world is not good

1575.reading: He tells his heart that men who painted musk on the chests of fair-browed women and slept on their shoulders as their lives quickened will suffer like birds that have lost their feathers, and go when their women cover their long lily-eyes.
1575.nuance: தூவியொழி புள்ளில் தோன்றி, 'appearing as a bird with its feathers gone', may be either old age or a rebirth; the verse does not say which.

claims.claim: those who sleep in women's arms come to suffering and death

1576.reading: He tells his heart that men who slept on soft beds full of sweet smoke on the shoulders of good women melting with love will go, their senses failing, when their own beloved, melting with love, cover their eyes.

claims.claim: the senses fail and the lover dies in the beloved's arms

1577.reading: He says that the one who wove bone with sinew, soaked it in blood, packed it with flesh, covered it with a thin skin, thatched it over with hair and made it a hut of flesh with nine doors is a cunning great carpenter, who makes the deluded more deluded.
1577.nuance: மன்பெருந் தச்சன் அல்லன் can be divided as நல்லன் ('is skilled') or அல்லன் ('is no'); with 1578, which names the builder வினைப்பெருந் தச்சன், the builder is the deed, not a god, and the praise of his skill is ironic.

claims.claim: the body is a hut of bone, sinew, blood, flesh, skin and hair with nine openings, built so as to delude

1578.reading: He says the deed is the great carpenter and a skilled one: when we begin to look at the truth it covers both our eyes as if the thing were ours, takes no account of those great in thought or those who have swum through learning, and so works that even the mind melts.
1578.nuance: The text of line 2 is damaged (see source_issues), so the sense of 'covers both eyes' is reconstructed. Read with 1574 to 1576, the eyes closed by the beloved at death and the eyes closed by the deed in life are the same image.

claims.claim: one's deeds blind a person to the truth about the body, and neither wisdom nor learning protects against it

1579.reading: As he sits so, the woman, thinking he will not melt at all unless she tells him how she came, begins: while she played in the forest among her bridal companions, a man went off like lightning cooling on a hill and rising to the top of the clouds.
1579.nuance: The narrator gives her motive before her story: she tells it to make him melt, so the story is offered as a means of seduction and may not be true.
1579.event: The woman begins to tell Civakan how she came to the forest.

1580.reading: She says a Vidyadhara carried her off as the young sun bears away a peahen while the flock scatters, his wife of unsleeping chastity saw it and had her thrown down, and she fell into this spear-sharp forest; her name is Anangamaa Veenai.
1580.nuance: In her account the wife's karpu is the force that removes a rival; துயிலிய கற்பு is unclear ('sleeping' or 'unsleeping' chastity) and may be ironic.
1580.event: Anangamaa Veenai tells Civakan that a Vidyadhara abducted her and his wife cast her into the forest.

links.note: The simile of 1557 sets Civakan's leaving beside men who renounce dancer and wife; 27 tells his final renunciation at the feet of the Knower.
links.teaches: Read together, the narrator's simile for a lover's journey is an early rehearsal of the end the patikam promises, so the hero already leaves his marriages in the manner of a renouncer long before he renounces.

links.note: In 1574 Civakan, tempted, asks his heart whether a world of women's pleasure ending in death is good; in 27 he hears the dharma and renounces.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the hero's renunciation has a rehearsal mid-story, but here the reflection serves only to keep his restraint against one woman, and he goes on to marry again, so the epic separates thinking renunciation from doing it.

links.note: Both list the body as a thing of filth with nine openings that dazzles the deluded; Naladiyar's fool is the lover, Civakan uses the inventory to refuse a woman.
links.teaches: The epic shows the Naladiyar's anatomy of the body being used by a man at the very moment of seduction, as a defence rather than a sermon, and by a hero who will still take wives, so the disgust is a tool of restraint, not a rule for life.

gains.a: Civakan's catalogue is placed in a known tradition of meditating on the body's foulness to cure desire, which marks it as a deliberate discipline and not a passing mood
gains.b: the quatrain's general mockery of the fool gets a speaker, a woman before him and a test, which it lacks, and the test is passed by one who is no ascetic

links.note: Arunagirinathar calls the nine-gated body a house Brahma built; the Cintamani's hut of flesh is built by a carpenter that 1578 names as the deed (வினை).
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows that the same anatomy of the body serves opposite accounts of its maker, a god in the Thiruppugazh and one's own deeds in the Jain epic, and that the disgust can be shared while the theology differs; the contrast rests on reading 1577's builder through 1578.

gains.a: the epic verse's unnamed builder is shown to be a doctrinal choice, since a devotional text with the same inventory names a creator god instead
gains.b: the Thiruppugazh's attribution to Brahma is shown not to follow from the inventory itself, since a text with the same list of body parts gives the work to karma

links.note: Tirumular's dead man has his nine gates shut while the loving ones weep and leave; the Cintamani's dying lover has his eyes closed by the beloved and goes.
links.teaches: The epic turns Tirumular's unnamed mourners into the very women of the man's pleasures, so the lovers who melt in his arms are those who close his eyes, which joins the critique of desire to the meditation on death.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains the Saiva verse's frame of the body's impermanence, showing the lover's death as one case of a general account of the body's end
gains.b: Tirumular's 'loving ones' (அன்புடையார்) are given a particular identity, the beloved of the bed, which makes his mourning scene a rebuke to desire as well as to attachment

links.note: The couplet holds that one's own understanding prevails however many subtle books one learns; the epic says the deed blinds those who have swum through learning.
links.teaches: The epic gives the limit of learning that the couplet states a cause and a scene, the deed covering one's eyes at the moment of desire, so the 'own understanding' that overrides books becomes the karma that defeats even the learned.

gains.a: the epic's claim that learning gives no protection is set against a known ethical rule about learning's limit, sharpening its point that knowing is not seeing
gains.b: the couplet's unstated reason why learning fails is supplied as karma at work in desire, one answer to the question its nuance leaves open

source_issues: 1557-1561, 1563-1570, 1577-1580: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build.
1571 lines 1-3 and 1572 line 3 contain stray '?' characters after சோ (சோ?), apparently a damaged character or a lost word in the e-text.
1578 line 2 begins புலெனக்குற்றுக் and 1579 line 2 begins புலொன்றுமற்: both look like a stray பு and a displaced final ல் from the line before (லுற்றால் எனக்கு; நல்லால் ஒன்றும்).
1562 line 3 முனை யுண்டவருருகும் is doubtful; the first word may be damaged.
1580 துயிலிய கற்பினாள்: the sense ('sleeping' or 'unsleeping' chastity) is unclear and may hide a misprint.
